The letter noted that the three companies reiterated positions emphasising user and parental agency rather than systemic regulatory intervention: Meta stated it does not collect or share usage data on children and maintained that time spent online is not a meaningful measure of risk; Roblox disclosed that children spend an average of 2.6 hours daily on its platform and that its Sentinel AI detects approximately 35 per cent of grooming cases proactively; TikTok outlined more than 50 automatic safety features for teenagers and confirmed it does not deliver personalised advertising to users under 18 in the UK. Hayes said the evidence reinforced the committee's conclusion that a widening gap remains between platform-led safety measures and the level of assurance required to protect children effectively online, and hoped the material would assist the government in its ongoing work.

Officials from the Home Office and the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport have run a work programme with Apple and Google to explore technical solutions on smartphones and tablets. The minister said the resulting proposals are a step in the right direction but do not meet the scale of the Government's ambition, and that the Government is therefore preparing primary legislation to require companies to build device operating system-level protections for children, alongside secondary legislation requiring apps used by children to prevent access to or sharing of nudity.
